messages.subject: Compensating for Over fitting variables
messages.body_plain:
Stefan,

I attempted to find the calculation you mentioned at AAAL but was unable to. If you could point me in the right direction that would be awesome.  Just to ask the group as a whole, we (psst.byu.edu <http://psst.byu.edu>) are researching correlations between our oral proficiency test and the OPI (Oral Proficiency Interview) and I'm trying to estimate how many OPIs we need to collect. Our test is approximatly 60 items and we currently have only 80 people that have taken our test and the OPI. I am trying to figure out how many OPI scores we need (along with their test scores on our test) so that we don't over-fit our model. Any suggestions would be welcome.

Thanks,

Ross

messages.body_plain:
Ross,

On Mar 26, 2009, at 11:45 PM, Ross Hendrickson wrote:

> yes that is exactly it, although the end goal is to create the best
> model to do prediction with.

If you care about accuracy rather than model simplicity and
interpretability, I would at least try an SVM (for regression).  R has
a simple to use SVM package called e1071 which will certainly be fast
enough for your situation.  (You may or may not need more data; I'd
try though.)

To avoid overfitting while maximizing the use of training material,
you could do cross-validation, training on all data points except one
(the one that is used for evaluation).   The same goes for a linear
regression model of course.

- David

--
Dr. David Reitter
Department of Psychology
Carnegie Mellon University
http://www.david-reitter.com

messages.body_plain:
David,

Thanks for the reply, question though: I have looked into k-fold cross validation measures, mainly when I was using WEKA to explore other options / models but am curious as to how cross validating eliminates the possible over fitting of the data. While searching for a solution to my sample "size" vs predictor problem I came across a calculator @ http://www.danielsoper.com/statcalc/calc01.aspx that is telling me that using the following desired attributes

Alpha: 0.05
# of Predictors : 60
Anticipated Effect Size (f squared): 0.35
Desired Statistical Power level: 0.8

I need a sample size of 139. My confusion arises because if I want a R squared of 0.7 (2.333 f squared) or higher the sample number changes to just 71. I'm not familiar with the f-squared value so I might be missing the point there.

As for the suggestion on the SVM, thanks for that and I'll look into it. I have played with the caret package and it has svm stuff however I havn't used the e1071 package and will explore its capabilities.

Thanks for the response,

Ross

messages.body_plain:
Ross,

> Thanks for the reply, question though: I have looked into k-fold
> cross validation measures, mainly when I was using WEKA to explore
> other options / models but am curious as to how cross validating
> eliminates the possible over fitting of the data.

Have a look at Andrew Moore's slides:

www-personal.umich.edu/~danjl/teaching/slides/cross_validation.pdf <http://www-personal.umich.edu/~danjl/teaching/slides/cross_validation.pdf>

SVMs are "large-margin classifiers" that use structural risk
minimization to minimize overfitting.  You'd still apply cross-
validation to them, particularly in order to estimate their parameters.
See also Tom Mitchell's slides:

www.cs.cmu.edu/~awm/15781/2003/Overfitting-MDL-StrucRisk.pdf <http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~awm/15781/2003/Overfitting-MDL-StrucRisk.pdf>

- David

messages.body_plain:
This works for your example, with "A"->10, "B"->11, etc. - is that
what you meant?

# your factor
set.seed(1)
the.factor<-factor(sample(LETTERS[1:4], 20, replace=T))
the.factor

# recode
recoded<-as.numeric(the.factor)+9
recoded

# check
table(recoded, the.factor)

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
